content: The parent company ceased the production of the drug due to reasons unrelated to tuberculosis (TB), leading to a global shortage of quality-assured formulations of this medication. A clinical trial conducted in 2014 evaluated a four-month standardized regimen for drug-susceptible TB, which included gatifloxacin (400 mg once daily). The study found no significant risk of hyperglycemia associated with gatifloxacin exposure. The frequency of serious adverse events (SAEs) linked to gatifloxacin was comparable to those associated with other fluoroquinolones in a study-level meta-analysis. Second-line injectable agents, based on available evidence, were associated with an increased likelihood of treatment success when included in longer multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) regimens. However, the small population size not receiving injectable agents limited the ability to detect the impact of this drug class. It is recommended that adults with rifampicin-resistant TB or MDR-TB receive a second-line injectable agent as part of their regimen unless there is a significant contraindication. In children with mild forms of the disease, the potential harms of these medications may outweigh the benefits, and injectable agents may be excluded. For children with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones, Group B medications should be retained. The choice among amikacin, capreomycin, or kanamycin depends on the likelihood of effectiveness and implementation considerations. Streptomycin, though not typically included as a second-line drug, can be used as the injectable agent in the core MDR-TB regimen if none of the other three agents are viable and if the strain is unlikely to be resistant to it. Adverse effects of second-line injectable agents must be carefully monitored. Hearing loss and nephrotoxicity are among the most frequent and severe side effects, though skin rash, hypersensitivity, and peripheral neuropathy may also occur. The risk of adverse effects increases with the cumulative dose of these agents, necessitating caution in individuals who have previously received these medications, including streptomycin as part of a drug-susceptible TB regimen. In children, hearing loss can significantly impact quality of life, language acquisition, and learning ability. A study on hearing loss in children with TB found that 24% of children treated for MDR-TB with an injectable agent experienced hearing loss, and 64% had progression of hearing loss after completing treatment. In this study, 30% of the children were HIV-infected. When designing the core MDR-TB treatment regimen, two or more of the following four medicines should be included: ethionamide (or prothionamide), cycloserine (or terizidone), linezolid, and clofazimine, usually in this order of preference unless the balance of benefits and harms for the individual patient suggests otherwise. Group C agents are added to ensure at least four effective second-line TB medicines are included in the core regimen during the intensive phase. If pyrazinamide cannot be included or relied upon, another agent is added. Ethionamide can be used interchangeably with prothionamide, and terizidone instead of cycloserine. Due to the lack of reliable drug susceptibility testing (DST) for Group C drugs, the choice of which ones to include is determined by the balance of desirable and undesirable effects and implementation considerations. The inclusion of cycloserine and ethionamide/prothionamide in MDR-TB regimens has shown an increased likelihood of treatment success in adults, though the evidence is less robust in children due to limited data. Linezolid has demonstrated statistically significant treatment benefits in both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies in adult patients, particularly in those with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). However, linezolid was used too sparingly in the included cohorts to allow a conclusive analysis. Adverse effects of ethionamide and prothionamide include gastrointestinal disturbances, particularly vomiting, which can limit tolerability. Hypothyroidism may occur, especially in combination with para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), but it is reversible upon cessation of the drugs. Cycloserine is well-known for its association with neuropsychiatric adverse effects. A meta-analysis comparing cycloserine with terizidone found no significant advantage of terizidone in terms of adverse effects. Linezolid's adverse effects include thrombocytopenia and anemia, which can be severe and life-threatening but are reversible upon drug cessation or dose reduction (typically from 600 mg daily to 300 mg daily). Hematologic toxicities are less common with current once-daily dosing strategies. Peripheral neuropathy may or may not improve after stopping the drug, and optic neuropathy should be treated as a medical emergency. Given the potentially serious adverse effects of linezolid, its use must balance risks and benefits and consider the availability of other TB medicines. Close monitoring for adverse events is essential when using linezolid. Where such monitoring is not feasible, linezolid should be reserved for MDR-TB patients with additional drug resistance, XDR-TB patients, or those intolerant to other core regimen components. Clofazimine likely contributes to the sterilizing function of MDR-TB regimens where pyrazinamide is ineffective. Although a single RCT showed a statistically significant treatment benefit with clofazimine, much of the evidence for its effect in MDR-TB comes from observational studies with conflicting or inconclusive findings. Skin discoloration or darkening is a common adverse effect of clofazimine, which may distress patients. In the RCT, adverse events were mostly limited to skin conditions and discoloration and did not lead to drug discontinuation. Serious adverse events appear to be relatively uncommon. Clofazimine may prolong the QT interval, so caution is advised when using it with other drugs that have the same effect. Add-on agents include drugs that do not form part of the core second-line agents. Group D1 consists of pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and high-dose isoniazid. These agents are usually added to core second-line medications unless risks from confirmed resistance, pill burden, intolerance, or drug-drug interactions outweigh potential benefits. Pyrazinamide has shown improved treatment success in some analyses, though its effect was not significant in others. Resistance to pyrazinamide is common in rifampicin-resistant TB strains, and reliable DST for pyrazinamide is often unavailable in resource-limited settings. High-dose isoniazid is recommended alongside a full MDR-TB regimen in patients with rifampicin-resistant TB strains confirmed or suspected to be susceptible to isoniazid. It is a core component of the shorter MDR-TB treatment regimen. However, in settings with high prevalence of high-level isoniazid resistance associated with katG mutations, high-dose isoniazid may be less effective, and its routine use may not be warranted. Group D2 includes bedaquiline and delamanid, two newer drugs released in recent years. WHO has issued interim policies on their use, and their role in children was under review at the time of these guidelines. Group D3 consists of PAS, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, clavulanate, and thioacetazone. PAS is reserved for situations where no other drugs are available. Carbapenems (imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem) are always used in combination with clavulanate. Thioacetazone has been largely restricted due to severe skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, particularly in people living with HIV. If thioacetazone is considered, close monitoring for severe skin reactions is required.
